The Spanish Flu. Between 1918 and 1920, a catastrophic global influenza pandemic killed an estimated 50 to 100 million people. Despite its name, the Spanish Flu did not originate in Spain. It was called Spanish because Spain, neutral in World War I, openly reported cases while combatant nations suppressed mortality data. The pandemic infected about one-third of the global population.

The virus was an unusually virulent strain of influenza A, the H1N1 subtype, that emerged in 1918. The first wave in the spring of 1918 was relatively mild. The second wave in the fall of 1918 was far deadlier, with victims dying within 48 hours of infection from pneumonia and cytokine storms. Mortality was highest among young, healthy adults, a pattern opposite to seasonal flu and suggesting an overactive immune response.

The virus spread by respiratory droplets. Crowded military barracks and transport ships during World War I created ideal conditions for transmission. Hospitals and medical systems worldwide were overwhelmed. Face masks and social distancing measures were implemented in many cities in response to the crisis.

The pandemic ended without a clear cause. Seasonal flu variants descended from the 1918 strain continue circulating today in less virulent forms. The crisis prompted major advances in epidemiology, vaccine development, and international disease surveillance. These innovations became the foundations of modern public health, shaping the disease reporting systems and quarantine protocols that remain in use today.
